ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a widely used plastic in various industries, contributing significantly to environmental pollution. Conventional methods for PET degradation are often associated with high costs, limited efficiency, and environmental harm. Consequently, biological approaches are gaining interest as sustainable, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly alternatives for PET degradation.

This study focused on the expression, biochemical characterization, and immobilization of a novel PET-degrading cutinase, known as PETase, isolated from Kibdelosporangium aridum (KaPETase). This enzyme presents a new thermostable alternative for addressing PET biodegradation at elevated temperatures. The cutinase gene from Kibdelosporangium aridum was transformed into Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells using the pET-22b(+) plasmid. The resulting recombinant KaPETase was purified by Ni-NTA chromatography, yielding a specific activity of about 6 U mg−1. The enzyme was immobilized in ZIF-8 and crosslinked with glutaraldehyde. The optimal pH and temperature for KaPETase preparations were determined to be 8.0 and 75 °C, respectively. In addition, the free enzyme maintained 80 % of its maximum activity at 100 °C. Through immobilization in ZIF-8, the catalytic efficiency and thermal stability of KaPETase were enhanced approximately three- and four-fold, respectively, PET degradation was analyzed using scanning electron microscopy and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, demonstrating the strong potential of both free and immobilized KaPETases for effective PET decomposition. Future research could focus on advanced in silico analyses, enzyme engineering, bioprocess scaling, and comprehensive assessments of PET degradation to further optimize this approach.

ce:section.ce:para: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a versatile synthetic polymer synthesized through chain polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid (Soong et al., 2022). PET is used in disposable textile products (Majumdar et al., 2020), beverage packaging and construction materials (Perera et al., 2019; Qaidi et al., 2022). PET is also widely used in medicine and healthcare, electronics, and the automotive industry. Its production has been increasing at a rate of 7 % from 2017 to 2025 (Singh and Bedi, 2023). This growth is driven by PET's exceptional properties, such as durability, stability, chemical resistance, transparency, and low susceptibility to hydrolysis at moderate temperatures (Fonseca and Taipa, 2024; Ren et al., 2024). Despite these benefits, PET waste accumulation is a major environmental concern. The persistent nature of industrial and household PET waste threatens ecosystems and public health (Qaidi et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2024). The challenges of PET degradation highlight the urgent need for innovative and effective mitigation strategies (Kawai, 2019).

A key challenge in PET biodegradation is its high glass transition temperature (Tg), which ranges from 75 to 80 °C in air and 65–70 °C in water (Ulaganathan et al., 2024). Therefore, cutinases that function above 60 °C exhibit significantly higher activity, although most common cutinases have an optimal range of 30–60 °C (Son et al., 2019; Sui et al., 2023). Well-known thermostable cutinases include LCC (LCCICCG), Cut190, TfH variant (TfCut2), and HiC (Sui et al., 2023). Thus, discovering novel thermostable enzymes and optimizing them for industrial applications are crucial for enhancing PET degradation (Son et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2021; Sintawee et al., 2012).

Enzyme immobilization is a promising strategy for enhancing stability and reusability. These techniques allow for enzyme separation from reaction mixtures, facilitating reuse, lowering operational costs, and promoting sustainable production (Jia et al., 2021). Various immobilization strategies have been applied to PET-degrading enzymes. Jia et al. immobilized PETase from P. sakaiensis onto nanostructured Co3(PO4)2 particles (PETase@Co3(PO4)2) and found that it exhibited greater pH tolerance than free PETase (Jia et al., 2021). Lee et al. immobilized PETase from P. sakaiensis as cross-linked enzyme aggregates (CLEAs), reporting that PETase-CLEA had a longer half-life than free PETase at 35–50 °C (Lee et al., 2024). Similarly, Han et al. covalently immobilized PETase on magnetic biochar, doubling its relative activity compared to free PETase (Han et al., 2024).

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are crystalline materials composed of metal nodes and organic linkers connected through coordination bonds. These materials are highly regarded for their exceptional properties, including 3D-ordered pore structure, ultrahigh porosity, and structural and functional tunability. Their flexible design further expands their applications. MOFs, are particularly promising for enzyme immobilization. Among MOFs, zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF-8) is one of the most extensively studied (Liang et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2022; Shomal et al., 2024). Its widespread use in enzyme immobilization is due to its low toxicity, high stability, and ease of synthesis under mild conditions (Zhou et al., 2022). Moreover, ZIF-8 offers a unique combination of high surface area and tunable pore structures, which can enhance enzyme loading and accessibility. Enzyme immobilization in ZIF-8 is occurs through encapsulation within its pores, formed by zinc ions and imidazolate ligands (Shomal et al., 2024). ZIF-8's stability across various conditions preserve enzyme activity over time, making it valuable for biocatalysis and biosensors. The versatility of organic ligands in ZIF-8 facilitates framework designs tailored to specific enzymes, potentially improving catalytic efficiency and selectivity. This research area is particularly significant for industrial applications requiring enhanced enzyme stability, reusability, and performance (Sowan et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2023; Shomal et al., 2024).

Recently identified PETases are valuable in combating the global environmental threat of PET pollution (Khairul Anuar et al., 2022; Burgin et al., 2024). Growing concerns over PET accumulation and ecosystem degradation due to PET accumulation have heightened research interest in these enzymes. Research efforts focus on discovering novel PET-degrading enzymes or optimizing existing ones for higher efficient and yield (Kushwaha et al., 2023). A major challenge in PET degradation is its high glass transition temperature, requiring thermostable enzymes for effective breakdown (Magalhães et al., 2021). The scarcity of thermostable, catalytically efficient PETases for in situ microplastic decomposition has prompted the search for new sources (Son et al., 2019). Few studies have examined the impact of ZIF-8 immobilization on PETases, despite its proven role in enhancing enzyme stability and activity. This study presents a highly thermostable PETase and evaluates the effect of MOF-based immobilization.

This study investigated a novel thermostable PETase from Kibdelosporangium aridum (KaPETase), heterologously expressed in E. coli and purified. Purified KaPETase was encapsulated in ZIF-8 and cross-linked with glutaraldehyde to enhance enzyme stability. KaPETase encapsulation was confirmed via scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and X-Ray diffraction (XRD) analysis. KaPETase preparations underwent comprehensive biochemical characterization including optimal pH, temperature, and kinetic parameters. The PET degradation capabilities of free and immobilized KaPETase were assessed using SEM and FTIR.

All chemicals and kits used in this study were of analytical grade, sourced from Thermo Fisher (Waltham, MA, USA) and Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells were obtained from Invitrogen (Waltham, MA, USA), while plasmid purification kits were provided by Zymo Research (California, USA). The culture auto-induction medium for expression was purchased from Formedium (Swaffham, Norfolk, England). Nickel-Nitrilotriacetic Acid (Ni-NTA) HisTrap column and disposable PD10 desalting column were procured from Cytiva (Marlborough, Massachusetts, US).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning of the K. aridum cutinase gene into pET22b(+) vector
ce:section.ce:para: KaPETase gene (UniProt accession number: A0A1W2FU08) was codon-optimized for expression in E. coli and commercially ligated into the pET-22b(+) vector at the NdeI and XhoI restriction sites. The enzyme was synthesized with a C-terminal hexahistidine tag (6xHis-tag), excluding the signal sequence.

A competent E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain was employed to express KaPETase under the pET-22b(+) vector. Transformation was performed using NEB®. heat shock transformation protocol. Recombinant E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells were plated on LB-agar (Luria-Bertani) (100 μg/mL ampicillin) and incubated at 37 °C for 16–18 h. Positive colonies were cultured in 5 mL LB broth (100 μg/mL ampicillin) at 37 °C and 180 rpm for 16–18 h. For protein expression, 200 mL of auto-induction medium (100 μg/mL ampicillin) in 1 L Erlenmeyer flasks was inoculated with 2 mL of pre-culture and incubated at 30 °C and 180 rpm for 16–18 h. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 4 °C, 5000 rpm for 20 min.

For purification, pellets were resuspended in 10 mL of lysis buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM NaH2PO4 pH 7.4, 30 mM imidazole, 1.0 mg/m lysozyme, 0.5 mM PMSF) and lysed by sonication (15 cycles of 15 s pulses with 15 s intervals) at 40 % amplitude using a Bandelin Sonopuls HD 2070 ultrasonic homogenizer (Berlin, Germany). The lysate was centrifuged at 10,000 rpm, 4 °C for 45 min, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.45 μm filter.

The N-NTA HisTrap column was equilibrated with ddH2O and buffer A (20 mM NaH2PO4, 500 mM NaCl, 30 mM imidazole, pH 7.4) before loading the supernatant. After loading, unbound proteins were removed with 5 mL of buffer A, and bound proteins were then eluted at 4 °C using buffers using increasing imidazole concentrations (100, 200, and 400 mM). Finally, 10 mL of buffer B (20 mM NaH2PO4, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 7.4) was used for complete protein elution.

Purified fractions were analyzed by SDS-PAGE using a Mini-PROTEAN II system (Bio-Rad, USA), and the gel was stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250. Fractions containing pure KaPETase were pooled, concentrated using 10-kDa MWCO ultrafiltration tubes, and subjected to buffer exchange using a PD-10 desalting column.

The protein concentrations were determined using a BCA assay kit following Thermo Fisher Scientific protocol. A calibration curve was generated using seven different BSA concentrations (0.1–2 mg mL−1) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2024).

p-Nitrophenyl acetate (p-NPA) was used as a model substrate to assess KaPETase activity. The activity assay was conducted by mixing 145 μL of 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0), 5 μL of 200 mM p-NPA (prepared in DMSO), and 50 μL of free or immobilized KaPETase at 50 °C. The formation of p-nitrophenol (p-NP) was monitored by measuring absorbance at 405 nm using a UV–visible spectrophotometer (Epoch Spectrophotometer, BioTek) (Fecker et al., 2018). One unit (U) of PETase activity was defined as the amount of enzyme catalyzing the formation of 1 μmole of p-NP per minute under these conditions (ε 405 for p-NP: 18,400 M−1cm−1). A blank control was performed under identical conditions without enzyme addition.

KaPETase immobilization in ZIF-8 was performed as described by Tülek et al., (2021). KaPETase solutions at different concentrations (0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 mg mL−1) were mixed with an equal volume (1 mL) of 1.0 M Zn(NO3)2 solution in water. The solutions were then added to 10 mL of 1.0 M 2-methylimidazole (2-MIM) solution water. The mixtures were gently shaken at 60 rpm at room temperature for 2 h. The resulting immobilized particles (KaPETase@ZIF-8) were collected via filtration, rinsed with distilled water, and stored at 5 °C. The filtrates were analyzed for protein content.

The crosslinking of KaPETase@ZIF-8 with glutaraldehyde (Glu) was performed. Briefly, 0.1 g of KaPETase@ZIF-8 particles were redispersed in 2.5 mL 25 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) containing glutaraldehyde at concentrations ranging from 0.625 to 5 %.The reaction proceeded at room temperature for 2 h. The crosslinked particles (KaPETase@ZIF-8/Glu) were then filtered, washed with distilled water to remove excess glutaraldehyde and stored at 5 °C. Immobilization yield (IY%) and recovered activity (RA%) values were determined as described (Tülek et al., 2021).

The morphological characteristics of ZIF-8 (without enzymes), KaPETase@ZIF-8, and KaPETase@ZIF-8/Glu were examined using SEM (Philips XL30 SFEG) at magnifications ranging from 5000 to 20000x. FTIR spectra of all KaPETase preparations were recorded using the Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) technique within wavenumber range of 500–4000 cm−1. XRD analysis of ZIF-8, KaPETase@ZIF-8, and KaPETase@ZIF-8/Glu was performed across a scanning range of 5–70 °C.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of free and immobilized KaPETases
ce:section.ce:para: The effect of pH on the activity of free and immobilized KaPETase was evaluated at 50 °C using different buffer solutions. Sodium phosphate buffers were used for pH ranges of 6.0–8.0, while Tris-HCl buffer was used for pH of 8.5 and 9.0. The optimum temperatures for free and immobilized PETase preparations were examined between 50 and 80 °C at pH 8.0.

To determine apparent Michaelis-Menten (KM) constants and maximum velocity (Vmax) for each KaPETase preparation, their activities were measured at pH 8.0 and 75 °C using different concentrations of p-NPA or p-NPB in the range of 0.1–4 mM. The apparent KM and Vmax values were estimated by plotting Michaelis-Menten curves using GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software Inc., 2022).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Thermal stability of free and immobilized KaPETases
ce:section.ce:para: Short-term thermal behavior of free KaPETase was investigated by incubating at different temperatures from 20 to 100 °C for 5 min. Additionally, the thermal stability of free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase, and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu preparations were assessed by measuring residual activities at 75 °C over a 24-h period. Residual activities were calculated by dividing the activity of each sample at a certain time by its initial activity. The thermal inactivation constant (kd), half-life values (t1/2), and stabilization factors (SF) of free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase, and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu were determined following the method described by Tülek et al., (2021).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Reuse and storage stability of immobilized KaPETase preparations
ce:section.ce:para: To evaluate the reuse stability, the remaining activity of ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu was measured in a batch reactor. A sample of 0.1 g ZIF-8@KaPETase or ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu was mixed with 3 mL of 10 mM p-NPA solution at 75 °C. After a 2 min reaction, the mixture was centrifuged (5000×g, 4 °C), and the absorbance of the supernatant was measured at 405 nm. After each cycle, the enzyme preparations was filtered and rinsed with 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer at H 8.0. The enzyme activity in each cycle was expressed relative to the activity in the first cycle.
The storage stability of ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu was evaluated by storing both enzyme formulations at 4 °C for up to 20 days.

The activity of each formulation was measured at various intervals during this period. The initial activity of both preparations was set to 100 %, and the residual activity at each time point was calculated by dividing the activity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: SEM and FTIR analysis of PET degradation
ce:section.ce:para: PET bottle was purchased from the local market, cut into 0.5 × 0.5 cm pieces, washed with distilled water (dH2O), and placed in Eppendorf tubes. The PET pieces were incubated varying concentrations of free and immobilized KaPETase for 1 day at 80 °C. For the control sample, PET pieces were incubated with 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer at pH 8.0 under the same circumstances. After incubation, the PET films were washed with dH2O and analyzed using HPLC (Shimadzu Prominence) and SEM (SEM, Philips XL30 SFEG). FTIR spectra were obtained for PET pieces that were incubated with free enzyme or buffer separately at room temperature for 28 days.

ce:section.ce:section-title: HPLC analysis of PET degradation products
ce:section.ce:para: Degradation products of PET were analyzed by HPLC equipped with a Wescan anion exclusion column (Alltech, 200 mm × 7.5 mm). Twenty microliters of sample were diluted with 80 μL of 10 mM H2SO4 solution and injected into the column. The mobile phase consisted of a 10 mM H2SO4 solution at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min, with the column temperature maintained at 30 °C. Degradation products were detected using a diode array detector at 205 nm. A calibration curve for terephthalic acid (TPA) was created by plotting its peak area concentration. The quantity of TPA produced by free or immobilized KaPETase was determined based on the corresponding peak area.

Several PETase enzymes are available in public databases. In the candidate gene selection process, P. sakaiensis served as a template organism due to its well-characterized PETase enzyme (Aer et al., 2022). Putative PETases with 40–60 % amino acid sequence similarity to the P. sakaiensis PETase were analyzed. Based on primary structure similarity and conserved functional amino acid sequences, PETase from K. aridum, an aerobic and Gram-positive bacterium (Shearer et al., 1986), was identified as a potential donor organism. This PETase shares 50 % sequence similarity with the PETase of P. sakaiensis (The UniProt Consortium, 2023) and has an estimated solubility value of 0.5, as predicted by Soluprot v1.0.

The sequence alignment results (Fig. 1 ) illustrate the primary structure of the enzyme, while the homology model confirms the correspondence of their three-dimensional (3D) structures (Fig. S1). The catalytic amino acid positions, indicated by arrows in Fig. 1, are highly conserved. Notably, position 87, which functions as a binding site, is Phe in K. aridum, whereas Tyr in P. sakaiensis (Joo et al., 2018).

The estimated molecular mass of K. aridum PETase, determined via UniProt, was approximately 30 kDa. Additionally, a potential signal sequence consisting of the first 23 amino acids was predicted using SignalP 5.0.
Purification analysis of heterologously expressed KaPETase in E. coli was analyzed using SDS-PAGE (Fig. 2 ).

Protein bands observed in SDS-PAGE analysis of purification fractions proved the presence and purity of the enzyme, which was revealed to have a molecular weight of approximately 33 kDa based on computational calculation. Similarly, PETase from P. sakaiensis has a comparable molecular weight of 29 kDa (Seo et al., 2019).

The immobilization of KaPETase in ZIF-8 were summarized in Table 1 . Three different initial concentrations of KaPETase were tested during the immobilization process. IYs were 100 % across all tested concentrations. However, RA (%) varied significantly depending on the initial enzyme loading, with values of 60.8, 92.3, and 45.3 % for protein loadings of 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 mg mL−1, respectively. The decrease in RA% at the highest protein loading (0.5 mg mL−1) may be attributed to formation of a protein barrier within ZIF-8, which likely hindering substrate access to the enzyme active site (Özdemir et al., 2024). Consequently, the activity of ZIF-8@KaPETase decreased at this higher protein loading. According to these results, ZIF-8@KaPETase with a protein loading of 0.25 mg mL−1 was selected for further experimental studies.

To enhance the robustness of ZIF-8@KaPETase, varying concentrations of glutaraldehyde were employed as crosslinking agent, as its concentration plays a crucial role in determining the enzyme's flexibility and activity. The glutaraldehyde concentrations used in this study were selected based on findings from previous research (Onur et al., 2022). The highest enzymatic activity was observed in the absence of glutaraldehyde, as illustrated in Fig. 3 . Increasing the glutaraldehyde concentration to 0.625 % reduced activity to 80 %, while a concentration of 1.25 % resulted in a relative activity of 85 %. A further increase in glutaraldehyde concentrations caused a decline in the activity of the immobilized KaPETase likely due to increased enzyme rigidity caused excessive crosslinking (Yildirim et al., 2014). Based on these results, the immobilized KaPETase preparation cross-linked with 1.25 % glutaraldehyde was selected for subsequent experimental investigations and designated as ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu. Onur et al. studied the effect of glutaraldehyde concentrations ranging from 0.625 to 5 % on the activity of epoxide hydrolase from Hypsibius dujardini encapsulated in ZIF-8, finding that optimal enzyme activity occurred at a concentration of 1.25 % (Onur et al., 2022).Metin girmek için buraya tıklayın veya dokunun.

XRD analysis results of ZIF-8 (control), ZIF-8@KaPETase, and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu are shown in Fig. 4 . The characteristics peaks of ZIF-8, ZIF-8@KaPETase, and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu at 20 values 7.33, 10.17, 12.46, 14.46, 16.16 and 17.67 correspond to the planes indexed for zinc atoms (011, 002, 112, 022, 013 and 222, respectively). These results indicate that the crystal structure of ZIF-8 remains unaltered after the immobilization of KaPETase (Alagöz et al., 2021).

FTIR spectra for ZIF-8, ZIF-8@KaPETase, and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu are presented in Fig. S3. The peaks at 688 and 755 cm−1 indicate the out-of-plane bending of the imidazole ring, which are characteristics of the ZIF structure and confirm the structural integrity of the ZIF-8 framework. The peaks at 2925 and 3185 cm−1 are attributed to the asymmetric aliphatic and aromatic C–H vibrations of 2-methylimidazole, confirming its incorporation into the ZIF structure. Additionally, the bands at 1750 cm−1 correspond to the C=O stretching of the amide I band, confirming the encapsulation of KaPETase within the ZIF-8 structure (Onur et al., 2022).

SEM analysis of ZIF-8, ZIF-8@KaPETase, and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu at various magnifications was conducted (Fig. 5 ). ZIF-8 displayed a regular crystal structure and smooth surface (Fig. 5A–C). In contrast, ZIF-8@KaPETase (Fig. 5D–F), and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu (Fig. 5G–I) exhibited an irregular crystal structure and rough surfaces, indicative of KaPETase immobilization (Tülek et al., 2021).

The effect of pH on the activities of free and immobilized KaPETase preparations was evaluated within a pH range of 6.0–9.0. The activities of the free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase, and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu increased as the pH rose from 6.0 to 8.0, reaching maximum activity at pH 8.0 (Fig. 6 A). Beyond this point, activity declined for all KaPETase preparations. At pH 9.0, free KaPETase lost 98.5 % of its initial activity, whereas ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu retained 73 and 81 % of their initial activities, respectively. These findings suggest that the immobilization within ZIF-8 provides protection against pH-induced denaturation. Comparatively, Yuan et al. reported an optimal pH of 7.5 for the free cutinase (ET-C), and 7.0 for its immobilized counterpart (ET-C@SiO2) (Yuan et al., 2023). Similarly, the optimum pH for both free and cross-linked enzyme aggregates (CLEAs) of PETase using amylopectin as a cross-linker (PETase-Amy-CLEA) was determined as 8.0 (Lee et al., 2024). Won et al. identified the optimal pH of cutinase from Antarctic Rhodococcus sp. as 9.0 (Won et al., 2022). Li et al. found that the optimum pH values of free PET hydrolase (DuraPETase) and its immobilized counterpart on Fe3O4 nanoparticles (DuraPETase@Fe3O4) were 8.0 and 9.0, respectively (Li et al., 2022).

To ascertain the optimal catalytic temperature of the free and immobilized KaPETase preparations were measured across a temperature range of 50–80 °C. All KaPETase preparations had a maximum activity at 75 °C (Fig. 6B). While only a few cutinase retain activity at high temperatures, enzymes from Humilica insolens (Ronkvist et al., 2009), Saccharomonospora viridis AHK190 (Kawai et al., 2014), Thermobifida fusca KW3 (Wei et al., 2019), Bacterium HR29 (Xi et al., 2021) have demonstrated activity at 60–90 °C. Notably, the KaPETase preparations showed 97 % of their initial activities at 80 °C. In contrast, Li et al. reported both free DuraPETase and its immobilized variant (DuraPETase@Fe3O4) had an optimum temperature of 60 °C but rapidly lost activity at higher temperatures, retaining only 26.0 and 35.3 % of their initial activity at 80 °C, respectively (Li et al., 2022). Similarly, Jia et al., found that free PETase and its immobilized counterpart (PETase@Co3(PO4)2) the optimum temperatures of 35 and 45 °C, respectively (Jia et al., 2021).

The thermal stability of KaPETase at elevated temperatures is a vital factor for the efficient biodegradation of PET, given that the glass transition temperature of PET is 65–70 °C in aqueous environments. The thermal stability of both free and immobilized KaPETase preparations was assessed at 75 °C over a 24-h incubation period. After this duration, free KaPETase maintained 50 % of its initial activity. Previous studies have indicated that various engineering approaches, including the addition of disulfide bridges, can enhance thermal stability (Zeng et al., 2022). Additionally, the presence of Met-Lys-His residues in the amino acid sequence may also influence this stability (Fett et al., 2000). A comparative analysis of the relevant residues and disulfide bridges was conducted among well-known bacterial thermophilic enzymes including Thermobifida fusca (optimal temperature: 60 °C) (Chen et al., 2008), Thermomonospora curvata (55–60 °C) (Wei et al., 2014), KaPETase, and P. sakaiensis PETase). Notably, P. sakaiensis contains two disulfide bridges despite not being classified as thermostable, whereas thermophilic enzymes typically exhibit only one. This analysis also revealed significant variation in the occurrence of Met and Lys residues among these enzymes. While P. sakaiensis shared a similar quantity of these residues, the number of His residues was markedly different in thermostable enzymes compared to P. sakaiensis PETase. Furthermore, superior conformational structures contribute to the thermal stability (Li et al., 2005). It was determined that previously mentioned thermostable PETase-like enzymes include nine α-helices and nine or ten β-sheets, whereas P. sakaiensis displayed eight α-helices and seven β-sheets. Baker et al. noted that the presence of neutral amino acids near active sites contributes to enhanced thermal tolerance (Baker et al., 2012). However, when comparing the amino acids adjacent to the active/binding site of KaPETase with those of P. sakaiensis, no transition from charged to neutral amino acids was found within five residues of the active/binding site. Another crucial parameter for stability is solvent accessible surface area (SASA) as reduced solvent exposure is associated with increased stability (Li et al., 2005). SASA calculations using PyMOL indicated that KaPETase had a SASA value of 13158 Å2, whereas P. sakaiensis PETase exhibited a value of 13526 Å2, this suggesting that the residues of KaPETase are less exposed to the water, potentially contributing to its enhanced stability. A comprehensive structural analysis is necessary to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the thermal stability of KaPETase, serving as a template for protein engineering studies aimed at improving PETase thermostability.

The thermal stability of various thermophilic PETases has been investigated. For instance, Thermobifida fusca Cut2 was expressed in an E. coli system, and its stability was assessed at 60, 70, 80, and 90 °C over 4.5 h (Ulaganathan et al., 2024). The enzyme half-life at these temperatures ranged from approximately 0.01 to 0.09 h, indicating substantial protection under experimental conditions. Notably, at 90 °C, the enzyme's half-life doubled. In contrast, Thermobifida cellulosilytica retained less than 30 % relative activity after 30 min of incubation at 60 °C (Jiddah Usman et al., 2023). Similarly, the Saccharomonospora viridis AHK190 Cut190 mutant (Ser226Pro/Arg228Ser) demonstrated an optimal temperature range of 65–75 °C but retained only 40 % of its activity after incubation at either 60 or 70 °C for 1 h. In comparison, the retention of approximately 45 % of activity for K. aridum cutinase at 80 °C is considered quite promising.

Additionally, a comparative study has demonstrated differences in thermal stability between free PETase and PETase-Amy-CLEA. Residual activities for free PETase were recorded at 71.5, 30.9, 13.9, and 17.0 % at temperatures of 35, 40, 45, and 50 °C, respectively after 60 min of incubation. In contrast, PETase-Amy-CLEA exhibited significantly higher stability retaining residual activities of 76.3, 69.4, 60.4, and 35.7 % activity under the same conditions. The half-lives of free PETase and PETase-Amy-CLEA were calculated as 87.7 and 128.4 min, respectively at 35 °C (Lee et al., 2024). Won et al. showed that cutinase from Antarctic Rhodococcus sp. immobilized on MA-DVB resin protected 52 % of its initial activity after 120 min of incubation whereas the free enzyme completely lost its activity within 10 min at 50 °C (Won et al., 2022). Jia et al. reported that the free PETase maintained only 17.2 % of its initial activity at 45 °C after 3 h, whereas immobilized PETase@Co3(PO4)2 protected 82.8 % activity under the same conditions (Jia et al., 2021).

Reusability is a crucial parameter for evaluating the industrial viability of a biocatalyst. In this study, the reusability of ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu was assessed using p-NPA as substrate under the optimum pH and temperature conditions. After 10 cycles of reuse, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu retained 90 and 93 % of their initial activities, respectively (Fig. 8 A). For comparison, Lee et al. reported that PETase-Amy-CLEA retained 43.1 % of its initial activity after the five cycle and lost its all initial activity at the end of the sixth cycle (Lee et al., 2024). Li et al. determined that DuraPETase@Fe3O4 retained 57 % of its initial activity after the six cycles (Li et al., 2022).

In this study, storage stability was evaluated by incubating ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu at 4 °C for 20 days. The results are shown in Fig. 8B. Both ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu maintained their full initial activities for the first 10 days. After 20 days, residual activities were 96 % for ZIF-8@KaPETase and 98 % for ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu, indicating excellent stability. In contrast, Lee et al. reported that PETase-Amy-CLEA retained 70 % of its initial activity after 40 days at 4 °C (Lee et al., 2024), while PETase@Co3(PO4)2 maintained 75 % of its initial activity after 12 days at room temperature (Jia et al., 2021).

The kinetic parameters, including apparent KM, Vmax, k
cat, and kcat/KM of free and immobilized KaPETase preparations against p-NPA and p-NPB are summarized in Table 3 . The apparent KM values were found to be 2.1, 0.6 and 1.2 mM for free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu, respectively with corresponding Vmax values of 16.7, 12.7 and 16.5 U mg protein−1. The calculated kcat values were 551.1, 419.4 and 544.5 min−1 for free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu, respectively. These results indicate that ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu exhibit catalytic efficiencies approximately 3 and 2 times higher than that of free KaPETase. For p-NPB, the apparent KM values were determined to be 0.53, 0.32 and 0.60 mM for free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu, respectively. The Vmax values corresponded to 15.5, 18.7, and 18.7 U mg protein−1. The kcat values were 511.5, 617.1 and 617.1 min−1 for free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu, respectively. These results show that the catalytic efficiencies of ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu are approximately 2 and 1.1 times higher than that of free KaPETase for p-NPB. Li et al. determined the KM, Vmax, kcat and kcat/KM values of free DuraPETase as 1.56 mM, 2.79 U mg−1 protein, 766.2 min−1 and 491.1 mM−1min−1 towards p-NPA. These values were 1.74 mM, 2.25 U mg−1 protein, 616.8 min−1 and 354.5 mM−1 min−1 for DuraPETase@Fe3O4 (Li et al., 2022). Lee et al. reported the KM, Vmax, kcat and kcat/KM values of free PETase were 10.1 mM, 0.66 U mg−1 protein, 0.02 min−1 and 0.002 mM−1 min−1 towards p-NPB (Lee et al., 2024). The corresponding values were 9.99 mM, 0.32 U mg−1 protein, 0.01 min−1 and 0.001 mM−1 min−1 for PETase-Amy-CLEA.

Enzymatic degradation, particularly through the use of PETase, has emerged as a promising avenue. In this study, PET pieces are treated with both free and immobilized PETases at different incubation times. Images were captured at different magnifications of 1000, 5000 and 10000x to assess surface changes. As clearly demonstrated in Fig. 9 , no noticeable alteration was observed on the PET surface for the control (Fig. 9A–C) after 24 h of incubation at 80 °C. However, treatment with free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu at a concentration of 0.1 mg protein mL−1 led to surface roughness, cracks, and holes on the PET surface under the same conditions, indicating effective PET degradation (Fig. 9D–L). Dong et al. performed a similar study by directly using Stenotrophomonas pavanii cells as an enzyme source, which resulted in morphological changes (Dong et al., 2020). In another study, Microbacterium oleivorans JWG-G2 and Thermobifida fusca cutinase were utilized in a synergistic way for PET degradation. After incubation of cells with PET samples at 35 °C and 120 rpm for 15 h, surface erosion was significant and supported by a combinatorial approach (Yan et al., 2021). Additionally, cutinase from Moniliophthora roreri was used to treat PET films in 100 U mL−1 enzyme solution at 37 °C for 21 days. The results demonstrated clear evidence of cracks, decomposition, and holes, consistent with previous studies (Laura et al., 2021).

PET pieces obtained after 28 days of incubation at 25 °C were also investigated using FTIR. As shown in Fig. S4A, the peaks of the control sample appeared at 1715 cm−1 (C=O stretching of carboxylic ester group), 1409 cm−1 (stretching of aromatic skeleton), 1251 and 1096 cm−1 (stretching of C–O group), 1096 and 723 cm−1 (in-plane C–H stretching and out-of-plane C–H bending of aromatic ring), which are characteristic of PET molecules. After KaPETase treatment, the intensity of the peaks decreased, indicating PET degradation (Fig. S4B).

The degradation products of PET catalyzed by free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu were analyzed using HPLC. After 24 h of incubation, the main peak detected was TPA (Fig. S5). The degradation rates were calculated to be 0.12, 0.43, and 0.14 μmol TPA mgmL−1 for free KaPETase, ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu, respectively (Fig. S6). These results show that ZIF-8@KaPETase and ZIF-8@KaPETase/Glu exhibit approximately 3.6- and 1.2-times higher degradation rates compared to free KaPETase, respectively.

In this study, a novel and thermostable KaPETase wase successfully expressed heterologously E. coli and purified. The highly purified enzyme was immobilized in ZIF-8, and the immobilized KaPETase was further cross-linked with glutaraldehyde. Biochemical characteristics of both free and immobilized PETase preparations revealed that their optimal pH and temperature were 8.0 and 75 °C, respectively. The immobilized KaPETase preparations exhibited significant thermal stability, retaining at least 90 % of their initial activity at 75 °C. PET degradation performance was investigated using SEM, which revealed crack, decomposition, and holes on the PET surface after treatment with both free and immobilized KaPETase preparations. Despite these promising results, this study has some limitations, including the lack of in-depth structural analysis and real-time PET degradation monitoring via HPLC or mass spectrometry (MS). Future studies should focus on deep structural investigations to elucidate the factors contributing to the enzyme's thermal stability. Such insights could provide valuable information for protein engineering and enzyme immobilization strategies, improving PET degradation at temperatures above 80 °C.
By addressing the stability and efficiency limitations of most PETases, this enzyme can serve as a model template for more targeted applications, improving industrial viability.
